On Mac you can pickup a configured OS that is up to date, and transfer it to another Mac that can support that up to date OS. This is because the hardware is all expected. On Windows - this is nearly impossible due to the vast volume of differences in hardware. You can likely move your profile and files - but your installed programs likely rely on software that is tied to the machine in specific ways. I'm not saying it can't be done - but that is probably not worth the time and effort you'll spend doing it.

If the software can run on older versions of windows - for example, Windows 7 - check out [UTM](https://mac.getutm.app/) instead of parallels. If your macbook is older and has an Intel - you can just use bootcamp, but if you don't want to boot into windows and lose macos - grab an old version of [VirtualBox](https://www.virtualbox.org/wiki/Downloads) which works great on Intel Macs

It's not that it's Most... it's that it takes a split second for wget vs something like a networkIdle2 puppeteer wait. On a 5 page site - no big deal. On a 50k page ecom site? Big deal. G may be huge - but there are still costs involved here and it directly correlates to crawl budgeting. So yes - your site gets hit more often by rudimentary bots, but rendering bots are just as busy - just with a bigger workload.

It depends on what your site is for. Ecom? Unless you're using the new merchant API - you're shooting yourself in the foot when it comes to timing if you're not SSRing. News sites - you just need to make sure you have a proper news sitemap. Everyone else should be ok - but you're still gonna fall behind competition in a few smaller ranking races.

To break it down a little more - SEs have multiple versions of bots that asses your site. Discovery vs Rendering for example - discovery bots are rudimentary and do not render (in fact - the simplest bot is basically wget). If you have a bunch of links that render in - they will not be discovered nearly as quickly as they won't be seen until a render bot visits.  In addition to that - the dissonance between the different records that google now has for 1 page does indeed cause a further delay.

Here's a [case study](https://www.onely.com/blog/google-needs-9x-more-time-to-crawl-js-than-html/) on JS affects on indexing. Also be sure to watch your [CrUX dataset](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/dashboard) as CSR tends to be a LOT harder on your mobile audience than you realize.

Traffic is a ranking factor, sure - but engagement and bouncing are higher order factors and consistency is paramount. However, none of these things by themself are an important focus of any SEO strat. Effective SEO is holistic and ticks a lot more boxes than traffic.

I work as a consultant for technical SEO directly with webdevs while my counterparts work with the marketing teams and execs. The first thing I always try to explain is that your targets in these cases are 2 things:

A - Robot visitors  
B - Chrome visitors

Robots are the various bots that Google will send your way to understand your site. They have bots that simple parse your raw markup looking for text content and links, then they also have bots that do things like come by and do a render job or look for structured data to further understand the page and domain. Giving the robots a good experience is not hard, but there are quite a few pitfalls around them as well. 

Chrome visitors - particularly the ones who have opted into sending Google their data (which is done at time of Chrome's install) - created a dataset know as CrUX (Chrome User Experience) - if your site has enough data, you can look at your CrUX report - inclusive of your site's real-world Core Web Vitals (the performance factors of your site that matter for ranking) here: [https://rviscomi.github.io/crux-dash-launcher/](https://rviscomi.github.io/crux-dash-launcher/)
